young.html: Candide is a kind, simple young man who grows up in a castle in Germany. His teacher, Doctor Pangloss, tells him that everything that happens is for the best, in "the best of all possible worlds."

Then Candide is thrown out of the castle and goes around the whole world. He meets storms, an earthquake, wars and many unkind people. Each time Pangloss says it was all for the best. Candide starts to wonder.

He even finds a hidden land called El Dorado, where gold lies on the roads like pebbles and everyone lives in peace. At the end Candide and his friends settle on a small farm. They stop arguing about big ideas, and Candide says: "We must cultivate our garden." Working together, they are finally content.

young.html: Plant a garden. Plant a seed in a cup of soil or tend a real garden patch. Each day, do one small job for it. Talk about Candide's last words: why might working on something small and real make people happier than arguing about whether everything is for the best?

full.html: Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), the most famous writer of the French Enlightenment: poet, playwright, historian and campaigner against intolerance and unjust trials. He published Candide, or Optimism in 1759, anonymously; it was banned in several places and sold widely anyway.

Its target is a philosophy of optimism, the claim, associated with the philosopher Leibniz and the poet Alexander Pope, that this is the best of all possible worlds and that every evil serves a larger good. The great Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which killed tens of thousands, had made Voltaire ask how anyone could say that to the people who suffered.

full.text:
Pangloss was professor of metaphysico-theologico-cosmolo-nigology. He proved admirably that there is no effect without a cause, and that, in this best of all possible worlds, the Baron's castle was the most magnificent of castles, and his lady the best of all possible Baronesses.

"It is demonstrable," said he, "that things cannot be otherwise than as they are; for all being created for an end, all is necessarily for the best end. Observe, that the nose has been formed to bear spectacles—thus we have spectacles."
full.author: Voltaire
full.ed: Candide, The Modern Library, Boni and Liveright, New York

full.html: Expelled from the castle for kissing the Baron's daughter, Cunégonde, Candide is forced into an army, sees a war, survives a shipwreck and the Lisbon earthquake, and flees to South America. In El Dorado he finds a peaceful, wise people who have no priests to quarrel and no courts or prisons; he leaves with treasure to rescue Cunégonde, and loses most of it to cheats. His companions include Cacambo, his loyal servant, and Martin, a gloomy scholar who thinks the world is mostly evil. Pangloss reappears again and again, battered but still insisting all is for the best.

full.name: gb-candide-map
full.cap: Candide's route, stop by stop. Each stop has its own target of satire.

full.html: In the end the friends live together on a little farm near Constantinople. A wise old Turk tells them that work keeps away three great evils: boredom, vice and poverty. Pangloss still makes speeches, but Candide has the last word:

full.text:
"There is a concatenation of events in this best of all possible worlds: for if you had not been kicked out of a magnificent castle for love of Miss Cunegonde: if you had not been put into the Inquisition: if you had not walked over America: if you had not stabbed the Baron: if you had not lost all your sheep from the fine country of El Dorado: you would not be here eating preserved citrons and pistachio-nuts."

"All that is very well," answered Candide, "but let us cultivate our garden."
full.author: Voltaire
full.ed: Candide, The Modern Library, Boni and Liveright, New York

full.html: Voltaire's method. Disasters come so fast and are told so flatly that the reader laughs, then notices what is being described. Each episode mocks something: war, religious persecution, greed, snobbery, and above all a philosophy that explains suffering away.

Reading the garden as giving up on the world. Many readers take it as practical advice: stop endless arguing about whether all is for the best, and do useful work that makes things better where you are.

deep.html: Leibniz's defenders point out that he never said each event is good, only that God chose the best world possible on the whole, with the fewest evils needed for the greatest good. Pangloss is a cartoon of that argument. Voltaire's reply, in effect, is that a theory that can explain every disaster as for the best explains nothing and comforts no one. Rousseau, later in this era, wrote to Voltaire defending providence after Lisbon; the problem of evil the two argued about is as old as the Book of Job and appears throughout this ladder, from Augustine to Dostoevsky.

items: Can good come out of bad things? Does that make the bad things good?
Why does Candide finally stop listening to Pangloss?
What does "cultivate our garden" mean for you?

questions: Pangloss says everything is for the best. Do you agree? Why or why not?
Why do you think Candide left El Dorado, even though it was so peaceful?
Who is wiser, Pangloss or Martin? Or neither?
What "garden" could you take care of in your own life?
Why might someone use jokes to talk about very sad things?

care: Candide is a short, fast satire in which wars, an earthquake and many cruelties happen in quick succession, told briefly and with dark comedy, and some scenes involve mistreatment of women. We summarize those parts without detail. Preview before reading it with children; the opening chapters and the ending in the garden are good to read together.
